📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since replacing Sepp Blatter amid a corruption scandal in 2016, FIFA president Gianni Infantino has solidified his grip on world football’s governing body.

He expanded the men's World Cup to 48 teams, introduced VAR, and has significantly increased development funding for member federations - a move that ensured his unchallenged re-election in 2019 and 2023.

Industry observers note that however, the political landscape has shifted this past year, following a fierce backlash against his aborted blueprint to sell stakes in World Cup profits to private investors. In short, Infantino’s uncontested reign is officially over.

Sources indicate that two football administrators have formally submitted their candidatures, securing the necessary backing from five member federations. When the 211 member associations vote in Morocco on March 18, 2027, Infantino will face two very different challengers.

Here is a look at the two men attempting to unseat him.

Industry observers note that philippe Diallo represents the most direct threat to Infantino. The 63-year-old took over as president of the French Football Federation (FFF) in 2023, and although a relatively recent arrival into the upper echelons of international football politics, he is a veteran sports administrator.

Backed by UEFA, who have spearheaded the resistance against Infantino, Diallo’s campaign is built upon reform and transparency.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Industry observers note that diallo has served on the UEFA Executive Committee and balanced domestic reform in France while overseeing a period of success for the national team and women’s game. He recently implemented a major grassroots initiative in France aimed at doubling registered female players to 500,000.

Diallo has lodged a direct attack on Infantino’s 'solitary governance', publicly questioning FIFA’s strategy of seeking private billions when the governing body already holds vast cash reserves.

“My vision is that of open governance,” Diallo recently stated. “It's one where the authorities truly play their role and the president is in charge of vision and strategy but leaves the day-to-day management to the secretary general.”.

From the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), Kohzo Tashima brings a different background to the election. Tashima, 69, is a former Japanese international who transitioned into coaching youth national teams before climbing the administrative ladder.

Tashima’s experience is embedded in the traditional structures of the sport and served as the president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024. He right now holds the title of honorary president. He has also served on both the FIFA Council and the AFC executive committee, earning a reputation as a reliable bureaucrat.

While Diallo focuses on the opacity of Infantino’s reign, Tashima's campaign hinges on a platform of restoring moral authority to FIFA.

Sources indicate that after his candidacy was officially submitted by the JFA, Tashima emphasised the need for a stronger sense of ethics at the top of world football. “We will share with the world the importance of fair play, respect and integrity,” he said. He has vowed to make FIFA a "healthier and more trusted organisation.".

The 2027 election in Morocco could be the most closely contested battle for the definitive seat of world football in generations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City have been dealt a multi-billion-pound blow, following their guilty verdict over breaching Premier League rules.

In September, an independent panel ruled that Man City were guilty of over 100 charges of breaking financial rules, with the Premier League confirming the verdict in an official statement.

Richard Masters, Chief Executive of the Premier League, described the case as “the most significant in Premier League history”, with the league's own statement using the word “sham” five times.

While the Sky Blues face uncertainty on the pitch – including whether or not they will be relegated from the Premier League as a result of a points deduction – there has reportedly been an impact behind the scenes, too.

The Financial Times reports that United States-based investment firm Apollo Global Management have abandoned a $2 billion loan to City owner Sheikh Mansour – worth just over £1.5bn – following the Premier League's verdict.

Talks were ongoing over the arrangement between The City Football Group and the private capital group, who manage more than $1 trillion of assets and have already dealt with the likes of Atletico Madrid and Nottingham Forest previously.

According to the report, “The loan from Apollo would have provided the group, which also owns clubs in Europe, the Americas and Asia, with extra liquidity as well as being used to refinance existing credit facilities, according to people familiar with the matter.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Filings at Companies House now indicate that Sheikh Mansour has invested £100m of equity into CFG via his Newton Investment and Development firm, following the Apollo collapse.

City are yet to feel the effects of the Premier League's verdict but have lost the last three matches in the Premier League after opening the season with seven straight wins.

The six-time champions responded to the news of the verdict with an emphatic 3-0 win over Liverpool at Anfield earlier this season, with the Anfield faithful bringing banners calling out their opponents.

Leading stars such as Erling Haaland, meanwhile, have been questioned over their futures, while former Citizens Manuel Akanji and Kyle Walker have both expressed worry that their titles could be revoked.

Manchester City host Fulham this weekend, as Premier League action continues.

  • Sources indicate that A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus: more speedy marathons by footballers, headed goals of the season and chairs acting as managers.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers.

It has been revealed that “Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”.

Sources indicate that A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

According to recent reports, but if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

But that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

According to recent reports, by our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

According to recent reports, the fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

The next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In Fresh York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

“Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”.

“The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”.

Peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”.

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

Martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I said, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”.

According to recent reports, with Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

It has been revealed that “He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”.

In a recent development, one of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:.

According to recent reports, “There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ mentioned Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” says Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”.

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

Recent findings suggest that “Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

“Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

It has been revealed that “Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

Man City boss Enzo Maresca says Erling Haaland had goal wrongly disallowed

  • The prolific Norwegian had an effort chalked off in the Premier League encounter at the Etihad Stadium when he was deemed to have kicked the ball out of Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno’s hands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Enzo Maresca had no doubt Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal in Manchester City’s 1-1 draw with Fulham on Saturday should have stood.

The prolific Norwegian had an effort chalked off in the Premier League encounter at the Etihad Stadium when he was deemed to have kicked the ball out of Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno’s hands.

Haaland had not connected cleanly with a volley but Leno spilled the ball attempting to gather his attempt and the striker prodded in from close range.

Referee Thomas Bramall, however, ruled that Leno – because the ball was still between his hands – had not lost control and VAR Sam Barrott upheld the decision.

Maresca mentioned: “I reviewed the goal after the game. From my point of view, it’s quite clear that it’s not a foul, but I’m not the guy that decides, unfortunately.”.

Asked how Haaland viewed the incident, Maresca added: “When they were reviewing the VAR, he was absolutely sure that it was a goal, because I asked him from the touchline. He was completely sure that it was a goal but the referee decided for different things.”.

With that effort ruled out in the 25th minute, City had to wait until just before the hour to cancel out Rodrigo Muniz’s 16th-minute opener.

Elliot Anderson scored their equaliser with a fine volley – a sweet moment for the midfielder after being sent off playing for England last weekend.

Maresca said: “It was a nice moment for him, a nice moment for us because it gave us the chance to come back in the game.

According to recent reports, “We used him today for the first time as an attacking midfielder. He was playing a little bit more deep with us. We are trying to find different solutions, the right balance, and to be more consistent.”.

Anderson’s equaliser ended City’s run of three successive Premier League defeats but it was nevertheless another frustrating result for a side that opened the campaign with seven straight wins.

Maresca stated: “For sure we don’t like this kind of moments, in terms of four games in a row without a win.

“But we also know that, unfortunately, it’s normal or it’s part of your path that you go through these kind of moments.

“It’s important that we find a way to keep a clean sheet. Sometimes you need to win games 1-0.”.

For Fulham, the result ended a sequence of 20 successive losses to City in all competitions and extended their unbeaten run to five games.

Manager Alvaro Arbeloa said: “We came here trying to win this match.

“Obviously we knew that we had lost the last 20 times against Man City, but I told them that we will have the chance to beat them if we play with courage, with character, if we press them so high, play the way we like to play.

Industry observers note that “I think we played really, really well. We could have won the game, but for me the most key thing was the performance and the character of my team.”.

After the international break, this is a transfer-heavy gameweek with players being bought and sold in bulk.

Whether you're planning on wildcarding or making wholesale changes and taking the hit, this is essential reading for all FPL managers getting back into the fantasy football groove.

Here is my verdict on the most popular names.

In a recent development, jan Paul van Hecke (£5.1m): One of the best defenders to own. He is guaranteed to play, reliable for defensive contributions and a threat from set-pieces. Spurs' next three fixtures are Ipswich, Sunderland and Fulham, which is incredibly solid. Verdict: BUY.

Recent findings suggest that luka Vuskovic (£5.3m): Brighton have kept the joint-most clean sheets this season, so he looks superb value. Maxim De Cuyper has grabbed the headlines, but Vuskovic is only five points behind and the second-highest scoring defender in the game. Strong defensive contributions, good attacking data and safe minutes explain it. Hull away, then Newcastle, Everton and Ipswich at home makes four of the next six fixtures too good to pass up. Verdict: BUY.

Ezri Konsa (£4.9m): Over 160,000 managers have bought him, which surprises me. He is a hold or a sell depending on your team, but never a buy. He is fine for a couple more gameweeks, but feels like a transfer out waiting to happen, as William Saliba is set for a return.

Recent findings suggest that I think the Frenchman is being saved for the Manchester City game in Gameweek 12. Konsa is worth owning if you already have Vuskovic and Van Hecke, but if selling him is your only route to either, make that move. Verdict: HOLD/SELL.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Industry observers note that lewis Hall (£5.2m): A poor defence and a tough run of fixtures. With Van Hecke and Vuskovic available, Hall is an easy sell. Verdict: SELL.

Josko Gvardiol (£5.6m): He costs a premium, and Manchester City are not in the best form for Expected Goals Conceded (xGC). He rarely earns defensive contribution points, so he relies solely on attacking threat. In my book, he's not worth it when the alternatives offer more, with zero headaches over minutes heading into the congested period. Verdict: SELL.

Marc Guehi (£6.0m): For similar reasons to Gvardiol, he is an easy sell, with no need to second guess starts of a player at this price every week. Verdict: SELL.

In a recent development, bryan Mbeumo (£7.9m): He has come close to returning several times in the last three gameweeks and been unlucky not to. Manchester United could get a fresh manager bounce, and from Gameweek 12 they face Brentford (H), Newcastle (A), Coventry (H) and Crystal Palace (A), so I would hold. Verdict: HOLD.

Kevin Schade (£6.1m): He has been a huge disappointment so far, but is worth holding onto. Igor Thiago is suspended, which should hand Schade penalty duties at home to Everton. He could be a smart differential. Verdict: HOLD.

Industry observers note that marcus Tavernier (£6.7m): Over 150,000 managers have bought him this week, which is understandable given Bournemouth’s fixtures. He is on four yellow cards though, and one away from a suspension, so I think he is worth dodging until the suspension risk is out of the way. Verdict: HOLD.

Joao Pedro (£7.6m): He is the most sold player of the gameweek at the time of writing. With his return close, I would stay put. Managers who swapped him for Nicolas Jackson or Thierno Barry have gained recently, but if you have kept him this long, Chelsea’s fixtures make it sensible to carry on. I do not own him, and I initiative to buy in Gameweek 13, as I expect him to be a good hold for the foreseeable future from that point on. Verdict: HOLD.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin (£6.0m): Recent returns have been underwhelming, so a lot of managers are getting rid. Leeds host Coventry in Gameweek 12, though, and with Erling Haaland away at Arsenal he could be a differential captain. I will bench him at Chelsea this week, play him in Gameweek 12, then decide in Gameweek 13. Verdict: HOLD.

#116941. WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1136 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw.
  • Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury.
  • Recent findings suggest that manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw.

Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager mentioned the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack.

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City.

Recent findings suggest that manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace. Maya Le Tissier stole the headlines with her goal on her 150th appearance for the club but the team’s improved defensive stability is also catching the eye and the centre-back is key to that. “For a defender you expect as the minimum you need to defend well and help to build,” mentioned the head coach, Eva Olid. “But now she’s scoring goals and that is more than a manager can ask from a centre-back. She’s in a high level and I’m so happy for her.” Le Tissier is showing consistent solidity and appears to be enjoying life under Olid now that things have settled, after seven goals conceded in their opening two WSL games. United have conceded four in eight WSL games since and are starting to show their flair. SW.

It has been revealed that have teams stopped fearing Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium? Their run of five consecutive WSL draws at home suggests so. London City Lionesses had 56% possession on Sunday and controlled the game for significant spells, especially in the second half, and although Arsenal created the greater chances, they do not play with the aura of a side attracting the largest attendances in the division. Renée Slegers was asked whether she was worried her team were losing that home “fear factor” and mentioned: “No, because we love playing at the Emirates. We had the biggest crowd so far in the season, the atmosphere was fantastic under the lights.” Probed further about her side’s home form, the head coach said: “I don’t think we’ve lost the fear factor, I think it’s a very hard place for oppositions to come.” Her side host West Ham next Sunday, looking for that elusive home WSL win. Tom Garry.

Match report: Arsenal 1-1 London City.

In a recent development, tottenham Hotspur were the latest team frustrated by Everton’s defensive solidity as they were held to a goalless draw. Despite controlling the ball and registering 17 shots, only three efforts were on target as they failed to score for the first time. Martin Ho was keen to highlight their opponents’ strengths as a key reason. “When we got into that attacking third, it was going to take something really special,” he told Spursplay. “They defended so deep with so many numbers behind the ball. You’re waiting for one of those moments to drop.” It was just the kind of performance fans have come to expect from Scott Phelan’s side. Unbeaten in their past three, in which they have faced Manchester United, Chelsea and Spurs, Everton have developed a strong resilience and character in recent weeks. Where they struggle is at the other end. Everton have scored eight goals this season (three of them own goals), higher than only Charlton in the WSL. Sophie Downey.

Liverpool ended their five-game winless league run with a statement victory over struggling Brighton, their third away win in 17 games. It has been a frustrating October and November block for Gareth Taylor and his team so there was much relief on the sideline that they were finally able to turn performance and opportunity into three points. Liverpool had less of the ball but their fast counterattacking proved too much for the Seagulls. A significant key to their success was Beata Olsson. She has six goals from her past five games in all competitions, stepping up when her team have needed it most. Injuries have kept out Aurélie Csillag and Ceri Holland for the best part of the season and Sophie Roman Haug is recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained 13 months ago. With limited attacking options, therefore, it will be very welcome that the Swedish striker has found her form in front of goal. SD.

Sources indicate that viviane Asseyi continued her impressive scoring form with a superb brace in West Ham’s 2-0 victory over Charlton, taking her WSL tally to seven this season. The striker opened the scoring with a composed finish from the edge of the area before producing the standout moment of the afternoon, curling a spectacular 25-yard free-kick into the top corner beyond Charlton’s goalkeeper, Anna Koivunen. Asseyi could have completed a hat-trick but her two goals proved decisive. West Ham’s head coach, Rita Guarino, described her as “an vital player”, adding that Asseyi was in a good goalscoring spell. Guarino felt Asseyi could have been happier with a hat-trick, but her latest double underlines her importance to West Ham’s attacking threat. Mitul Samji.

Poor officiating dominated the narrative of the second city derby as Aston Villa edged Birmingham City 1-0, with both sides feeling hard done by. First, City felt Lucy Parker had fouled Océane Hurtré in the penalty area in the 24th minute, only for the referee to award a corner. Whether the incident was inside the box was disputable, but it did appear to be a foul. Minutes later, Villa had a goal from Océane Deslandes overruled for what was declared a foul on the goalkeeper in another contentious call, but they managed to find a winner in the second half. The two things Roberto De Zerbi demanded from Luca Williams-Barnett's first Tottenham start as 18-year-old star eyes newly introduced lucrative deal with clubs circling, writes MATT BARLOW

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 08:08 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 08:10 EST, 22 November 2026.
  • Having summoned Luca Williams-Barnett to his office to let the teenager know he would be making his first Premier League start, Roberto De Zerbi could not resist a little bit of fun.
  • De Zerbi cast a serious demeanour and told him he had weighed the options and figured the best course of action would be 60 minutes with the Under-21s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER.

Published: 08:08 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 08:10 EST, 22 November 2026.

Having summoned Luca Williams-Barnett to his office to let the teenager know he would be making his first Premier League start, Roberto De Zerbi could not resist a little bit of fun.

De Zerbi cast a serious demeanour and told him he had weighed the options and figured the best course of action would be 60 minutes with the Under-21s.

Recent findings suggest that williams-Barnett did not hide his disappointment. 'Why, do you think you are ready to start for the first team?' asked the Spurs boss. The 18-year-old said he thought so.

De Zerbi cracked a smile and told him he was in the team against Ipswich but demanded two things in return.

First, that his young star would play with freedom as though 'in the park with friends' and second that he would work without the ball in the manner of the world's best players in his position, such as Lamine Yamal.

Industry observers note that this is where the comparisons to Yamal emerged soon after Williams-Barnett lit up the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Similarities are evident in physique, his fluency of movement on the ball and the bursts of pace, the way they look to play. Even the hairstyle.

Just as Yamal, a left footer, likes to operate wide on the right for Barcelona and Spain, De Zerbi deployed Williams-Barnett as a right footer on the left, although most of his youth career has been spent centrally in the No.10 position.

Luca Williams-Barnett scored his first Premier League goal for Tottenham on his first start in the top flight.

The talented academy youngster may not be lightning fast but he has pace and creates goals.

He does not possess what you would consider in modern football to be exceptional pace, but he is quick, and his strengths are on the ball. He likes the ball. He creates. And he scores goals.

From wide on the left against Ipswich, he scored within 15 minutes, darting in at the back post to finish, and created the second for Dominic Solanke, with a 60-yard run from inside his own half and cross with his left foot.

His brilliance lit up the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, where there has not been a lot to celebrate in the last 18 months. Terrible home form was the crux of last season's relegation fears.

In a recent development, here, they rose to salute a latest talent, one of their own. One De Zerbi believes has the attitude to match his outrageous talent. Confident, certainly. Aware of his natural gifts and his technical skills. Perhaps bordering on arrogance when on the pitch.

De Zerbi was pleased to see Williams-Barnett, in a seat nearby on the team bus from the training ground to the stadium, watching YouTube clips of Ronaldinho, Eden Hazard and Neymar.

According to recent reports, the Spurs boss, who has faith in the power of inspirational video footage, took this as a positive sign. The youngster was relaxed but more than this he had a passion for football and always looking to learn.

'I'm positive about his character and behaviour because I've been working with him for three or four months and I know him enough,' said De Zerbi, whose tactical instructions involved James Maddison operating closely to Williams-Barnett, a kindred spirit in a footballing sense able to talk him through the game.

When the teenager set off on the swaggering run for Solanke's goal, Maddison could be seen nearby urging him forward into the ocean of space left open by Ipswich.

Spurs have prioritised Premier League experience in the transfer market under De Zerbi to create a more mature dressing room environment. Signings such as Andy Robertson have been key to this.

The policy is not purely for the benefit of academy graduates stepping into the first-team environment, but it does help when it comes to setting the standards required in elite sport.

Anyone gifted enough to break into the Spurs squad will have been feted as a star through the youth development phase and well rewarded to resist others trying to lure them away.

Currently under contract until 2028, the 18-year-old has rival clubs circling if Spurs cannot pin him down.

Born and raised in Luton, Williams-Barnett comes from a strong, grounded family - which will only help as he looks to assimilate into the senior side.

Williams-Barnett is under contract until 2028 but is understood to be closing in on a lucrative newly introduced deal to tie him down because others have been circling.

It is easy for impressionable teens to become conceited in this situation. Williams-Barnett has had discipline and time-keeping issues but most at Spurs speak of a young man devoted to his football from a strong, loving family who are sure to keep him grounded.

He was born and raised in Luton, starting out in Luton Town's pre-academy to Under 10s, before Spurs paid a small fee for him.

His father Jonathan Barnett was a central midfielder in Step Three of non-league football, known as 'Jono' and playing for various clubs in the region including Dunstable Town and Arlesey Town and renowned for his passing, set pieces and with an eye for goal.

Although more of a dribbler, Luca grew up with football in the family, polishing his technical skills with his dad in the back garden. 'He is from a very good family and it's crucial for this type of players,' noted De Zerbi.

Spurs have been here before, of course, with talented teens breaking through with N17 at their feet.

There was Mikey Moore's wonderful cameo against AZ Alkmaar after which Ange Postecoglou called for patience and commonsense, and Maddison went on TV and noted it was 'like having Neymar on the left wing'.

There was Jose Mourinho taking the match ball from Son Heung-min, who had just scored the most incredible solo goal against Burnley and handing it to Troy Parrott on his Premier League debut.

Recent findings suggest that there was Mauricio Pochettino dubbing Marcus Edwards his 'Mini Messi'. Pochettino soon came to wish he had not burdened Edwards with such lavish praise.

The pitfalls are well known and progress is rarely a smooth upward trajectory. It is a balancing act between maximising potential and getting carried away.

De Zerbi is quietly confident Williams-Barnett has what it takes to handle the hype.

These gaps in weather data affect forecasts everywhere: plugging them is not charity

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that observations from data-scarce regions, such as low-lying island Tuvalu in the South Pacific, are crucial to weather forecasts, early warning systems and climate-information services elsewhere.
  • When I talk about collecting essential weather and climate data in countries with limited resources, many take it to mean that wealthier countries, institutions and firms should ‘help poorer ones’.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s the resounding conclusion of a report published this month by The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in collaboration with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that observations from data-scarce regions, such as low-lying island Tuvalu in the South Pacific, are crucial to weather forecasts, early warning systems and climate-information services elsewhere. Credit: Mario Tama/Getty.

When I talk about collecting essential weather and climate data in countries with limited resources, many take it to mean that wealthier countries, institutions and firms should ‘help poorer ones’. But as a development and climate-finance executive, I know that this is an investment rather than an act of charity. Science proves it: better forecasts at home rely on observations abroad.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the resounding conclusion of a report published this month by The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in collaboration with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). The report was commissioned by the Systematic Observations Financing Facility (SOFF), a United Nations fund dedicated to basic weather and climate data around the world, of which I am a director.

Sources indicate that its aim was to establish the benefits of filling gaps in the WMO’s Global Basic Observing Network (GBON), which defines member nations’ mandatory weather-station coverage. To comply, each country must have a land station every 200 kilometres, as well as a weather balloon every 500 kilometres over land and every 1,000 kilometres over sea to collect data on essential variables (such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind).

Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved.

Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved.

Recent findings suggest that but agreeing on standards and sites is not the same as having the economic means to implement them. Since 2023, GBON stations have been required to share their data. Yet, about 90% of weather data from low-income countries and small island nations are not being shared. Some data are not even collected because many stations are missing, stopped working or cannot transmit their measurements.

It has been revealed that these gaps don’t just impede local forecasts, they affect regional and global projections too. Daily weather data feed into increasingly sophisticated computer models that predict how weather systems around the world evolve.

In a recent development, think of a weather forecast as a photograph. It is made up of millions of pixels, each contributing a small piece of information. Weather forecasting is more complex, but the analogy helps to explain the problem: if too many ‘pixels’ are missing, the global picture is blurry or incomplete. And for forecasts, some ‘pixels’, or observations, are more valuable than others. Plugging gaps in data-scarce regions is the best way to improve forecasts everywhere.

According to recent reports, it is also a matter of justice: on average, a seven-day temperature forecast in a high-income country is as accurate as a one-day forecast in a low-income country (M. Linsenmeier and J. G. Shrader Nature Commun. 17, 10792; 2026).

The results of the ECMWF simulations are striking. Better coverage in low-income countries and small island states can cut uncertainty in 12-hour local forecasts by more than 30% in parts of Africa and by up to 20% across the Pacific.

In a recent development, extra data in all countries eligible for development assistance and small island nations would improve the accuracy of temperature and wind forecasts up to six or seven days ahead in the tropics, home to some 40% of the world’s population, and in the Northern Hemisphere’s mid-latitudes, where much of Europe, North America and northern Asia sit. This would help with, for example, aviation and maritime operations, planning of agricultural activities, water management and preparations for severe weather.

Disparity in countries’ capacity to finance weather observations is striking. To quantify the inequality, SOFF developed an indicator comparing countries’ gross dom-estic product (GDP) with the geographical area for which they are mandated to provide observations, including marine exclusive economic zones. For example, although it is a small country, Switzerland has a larger budget than does Tuvalu, a Pacific island nation spread across an immense ocean area (Switzerland’s GDP is around 300,000 times larger per square kilometre). Yet both countries contribute to and benefit from the same global observing system.

#116933. Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1058 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal.
  • But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
  • According to recent reports, as a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.

But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.

According to recent reports, as a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.

They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).

Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.

The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.

Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find new forms of income.

A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.

Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.

It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.

"I think it's more of a long-term game," stated Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.

It has been revealed that she states it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.

One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels.".

She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.

The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.

This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.

Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national prepares to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no upcoming commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.

It has been revealed that kumar states more countries could announce similar aims just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.

Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.

The nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.

The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.

The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.

Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.

This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any massive announcements about fossil fuels.

Recent findings suggest that global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.

A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald demonstrates that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing upcoming reserves.

Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.

One concern Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.

The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.

Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.

"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum.".

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mikel Arteta said that goalkeeper David Raya will undergo an MRI scan on his injured shoulder as the Gunners boss lamented his side dropping two points following a 2-2 draw at Newcastle.

Eberechi Eze put Arsenal ahead just past the half hour and he saw a free-kick saved on the stroke of half-time after Noni Madueke spurned a couple of chances to put the visitors further in front.

But Newcastle, booed off at the break, rallied on the resumption and Martin Odegaard being dispossessed from a throw-in allowed Harvey Barnes to score while Dan Burn’s free header from a corner caused a goalmouth scramble and Malick Thiaw capitalised to poke home from a yard out.

Arsenal then lost goalkeeper Raya to injury, although they claimed a share of the spoils thanks to Madueke 12 minutes from time as the Premier League leaders moved six points clear of Brighton, who could halve the deficit when they play at Hull on Sunday.

Arteta said: “My feeling is we have lost two points. We were exceptional in the first half from the beginning to the end. We should have been two, three or four-nil up clearly.

According to recent reports, “When you don’t do that then the opponent is going to try to react and right from the beginning (of the second half) we weren’t at the races. One thing is to give them belief and another thing is to give them a goal. We did both.

Industry observers note that “After that, we came back and we were exceptional. We scored the second goal and we had opportunities to go and kill the game. We lacked a moment of magic to be able to do that.

Industry observers note that “It’s a pity because the margin should have been much bigger for the level we demonstrated. I never remember that we played at that level here, never. We have won football matches playing much worse than we did today here.”.

Raya was forced off in the 70th minute, having received treatment when he slumped to the floor after coming out to collect a corner, and left the field clutching his arm with an apparent shoulder problem.

In a recent development, arteta stated: “Unfortunately, he had to come off, which is never good news. He will get assessed now and he will probably have an MRI tomorrow to see what it is exactly because at the moment, I don’t know.”.

Bruno Guimaraes also made way when Raya was withdrawn, with the former Newcastle midfielder’s every touch heavily barracked on his first return to Tyneside since his £75m move in the summer.

Arteta, though, spoke favourably of the Brazilian’s performance, adding: “It’s never easy, emotionally, you have so much going on, especially the way he feels connected to this club. But I thought he had a very good performance.”.

Matthias Jaissle reflected on a performance of two halves – but Newcastle’s head coach hopes they can take their second 45-minute display into the rest of the season.

The German said: “It was pretty clear in the first half we were not that front-foot or that intense, somehow hesitating to make the last step or last yard.

According to recent reports, “This is something you can’t afford against a top team. But the second half was pure belief, pure conviction, no hesitation any more, pure trust between the team-mates that they are doing their jobs.

“This is the Newcastle DNA and I hope we can build on the second half.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Edwin van der Sar has his wife to thank for rapidly spotting the symptoms when he suffered a brain haemorrhage in 2023.

The former Ajax, Juventus, Fulham and Manchester United great has since gone on to make a full recovery, and appeared for an Ajax Legends side against their Barcelona counterparts at the Johan Cruyff Arena last weekend.

But at the time it happened, Van der Sar's wife, Annemarie van Kesteren, knew exactly what was happening having suffered a brain haemorrhage herself back in 2009.

Van der Sar told FourFourTwo: "Annemarie knew what was happening. I had this strange feeling that something wasn't right.

"Then before you know it, you see the light and the light hurts your eyes. I had pain in my head.

"From that point onwards, you just let yourself go, and hope the ambulance and the people around you take care of you.

"You have to put your faith, your life, into the hands of people who are trained for that and who specialise in it.".

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In a way, Van der Sar considers the timing to be fortuitous: he had only recent resigned as Ajax chief executive after seven years in the post.

He said: "I'd stepped away five or six weeks before [from Ajax], so I had all the time in the world to recover, rest and get better.

"If I'd still had the job, I think the eagerness and the demands of the position might have made my recovery harder.

"When you're responsible for a club, a firm or an organisation, you want to be there.

"Luckily, I had no ties and nothing else to focus on apart from myself and my recovery. I've had a few chats - but nothing has really felt right.

"I'm enjoying my life at the moment, and I'm not actively looking for another position.".

Sources indicate that steven Chicken has been working as a football writer since 2009, taking in stints with Football365 and the Huddersfield Examiner. Steven still covers Huddersfield Town home and away for his own publication, WeAreTerriers.com. Steven is a two-time nominee for Regional Journalist of the Year at the prestigious British Sports Journalism Awards, making the shortlist in 2020 and 2023.

Roberto De Zerbi compares Luca Williams-Barnett to Lamine Yamal after Tottenham win

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi was not surprised by a dazzling full debut display from “special” talent Luca Williams-Barnett and compared the 18-year-old to Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal after Saturday’s 2-0 win over Ipswich.
  • De Zerbi turned to the highly-rated Spurs academy graduate after two bright cameos and he delivered with aplomb, scoring on his first Premier League start after 15 minutes before a mazy run set up Dominic Solanke at the start of the second half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi was not surprised by a dazzling full debut display from “special” talent Luca Williams-Barnett and compared the 18-year-old to Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal after Saturday’s 2-0 win over Ipswich.

De Zerbi turned to the highly-rated Spurs academy graduate after two bright cameos and he delivered with aplomb, scoring on his first Premier League start after 15 minutes before a mazy run set up Dominic Solanke at the start of the second half.

After Williams-Barnett made his senior debut at the age of 16 last season, the clamour for the teenager to play has only increased during a difficult last 12 months and De Zerbi decided 10 days ago to include him in the starting line-up against Ipswich.

During a chat on Thursday with the skilful England Under-19 international, De Zerbi asked Williams-Barnett to play with freedom and work hard without the ball “like Raphinha, like Yamal” before he agreed when asked if the teenager could reach similar heights.

After De Zerbi revealed Williams-Barnett prepared for the match on the team bus by watching YouTube clips of Ronaldinho, Eden Hazard and Neymar, he said: “Luca is a special player.

According to recent reports, “I’m not surprised, because his talent is bigger than you think. He played very well. I think he’s lucky, because he’s playing in a top club, with top team-mates.

“I decided to play today with Luca from 10 days and in my initiative, it was (James) Maddison and Luca very close to speak the same language, to play together and the experience of Maddison I thought could be important.

“The behaviour of Maddison could help him to play with freedom. And Thursday, I spoke with Luca and I asked him two things. Just two things. To play like he plays on the park with his friends, with the same freedom.

“And to play and to work hard without the ball, like (Ousmane) Dembele, like Raphinha, like Yamal, because football is going in a different way and the first defenders are the attackers.

“Even if they are Ballon d’Or winners, or any way the players with talent, they have to work on the pitch.”.

Asked if Williams-Barnett can reach the level of Yamal, De Zerbi said: “Yes, I think so.

“And one of the best things in my career… I’ve seen today in the bus from the training ground to the stadium, because he was very close with me, while we were coming in the stadium, he was watching on YouTube Ronaldinho, Hazard, Neymar.

Recent findings suggest that “I thought he was a special guy, because if one hour and thirty minutes before you are debuting in the Premier League, you are watching Ronaldinho, Hazard, Neymar, all these types of talent. The football is magic, no?”.

Gary O’Neil watched Ipswich’s winless run extend to five matches.

Industry observers note that “Many of us weren’t quite able to get to the level that we’re used to. A tough afternoon. I didn’t enjoy it but I did enjoy watching the lads dig in and find a way to keep going together in a tough moment because that’s what we need,” O’Neil mentioned.

“Between the goals and after the goals, we were OK and we arrived in the final third enough to cause problems but we didn’t. Disappointing but it was a major task coming here and we needed things to be perfect.”.

Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more.
  • Sources indicate that “The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic.
  • Recent findings suggest that the gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers.

Sources indicate that “The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic. “Is this the biggest gap between the best and worst ranking for one national team?”.

Recent findings suggest that the gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. Wales and Northern Ireland both moved up 109 places: Wales from 117th to eighth under Gary Speed and then Chris Coleman, Northern Ireland from 129th in 2004 to 20th in 2017.

Sources indicate that it is the speed of Scotland’s improvement that was most notable. “At two years, seven months and one day that feels like quite the rise,” writes Robbie Dale. “A look at the data highlights it is bettered by only nine other countries. Colombia’s rise from a low of 51 to a high of 12 in exactly two years [between 2016 and 2018] is one notable example. Dominica and Kenya rose up the ranks by 70 and 69 places respectively over the course of just 16 months.”.

In a recent development, some of the biggest movers are countries who joined Fifa after the men’s rankings were introduced in 1992, which means they started at the bottom. “I immediately thought of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” writes JJ Galbraith. “They were ranked 173rd in 1996, shortly after playing their first game as an independent nation. Their pinnacle was 13th place in 2013 – a rise of 160 places.”.

That 160-place gap is beaten by only two teams. Kuwait reached 24th in the Fifa rankings in 1998, when they won the Arabian Gulf Cup in style and finished second at the Asian Games. By 2017 they were 189th in the world, a difference of 165 places.

According to recent reports, that is 18 places short of the record. “Montenegro were ranked 199th when they played their first international match in 2007,” writes Pete Tomlin. “In 2011 they managed to climb up to 16th, thanks to some strong results in Euro 2012 qualifying (victories against Wales, Bulgaria and Switzerland and a 0-0 draw with England at Wembley).”.

Thanks to Pete, Mark Holt, Cameron McGlone, Sean DeLoughry and others for helping us compile this list of the biggest movers.

183 places Montenegro (16th/199th).

160 Bosnia and Herzegovina (13/173).

153 Central African Republic (49/202).

136 Cuba (46/182), Slovakia (14/150).

Sources indicate that pete Tomlin has also crunched the numbers for the women’s game. “The gaps are much smaller,” writes Pete, “due to the fact that the rankings have only been recorded since 2003, there are fewer teams and many of the national sides play very few matches.

It has been revealed that “The biggest gap belongs to the Bahamas with a high of 96th and a low of 194th, a difference of 98 places. There are actually two women’s teams with a gap of zero, but this is because they have played so few games. Chad (156th) and Sudan (194th) have never moved.”.

“Non-league minnows Plymouth Parkway reached the second round of the FA Cup the other weekend,” writes Jon Archer. “I noticed their club crest appears to feature a road going under a bridge. Are there any other clubs who have roads on their badge?” Indeed the Southern League Premier Division South side have the A38 on their crest, a nod to, erm, the nearby stretch of dual carriageway that helps give the club its name via their former ground at the Parkway Sports Club.

According to recent reports, it is not a common occurrence and somewhat depends on how far you want to stretch things. Sunderland, for example, have a section of the Wearmouth Bridge on their crest, which certainly carries a road, though it is not visible. Similarly National League South’s Maidenhead United redesigned their badge in 2020 to celebrate the club’s 150th anniversary – it features a stretch of the town’s Thames river bridge, a nod to where the club played their first game back in 1870, which now carries the A4. Farther afield the German minnows TSG Backnang’s crest features the Murr Valley viaduct, which both overlooks the team’s ground and carries the B14, which links Stuttgart and Nuremberg.

Those might be a bit of a reach, but, far more definitively, across the West Country from Plymouth Parkway are tiny eighth-tier Willand Rovers of the Southern League Division One South. Their badge is a proper old shield effort featuring the River Culm, a castle tower … and the M5 motorway, which slices through the village to the north.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

Recent findings suggest that the answers above put Liverpool on two titles per manager and their great rivals down the M62 on 6.66 titles per manager (which is doing Alex Ferguson a great disservice but we have to find a way to make this question work). Daz Pearce offers up one-title-one-manager wonders Leicester (Claudio Ranieri), Nottingham Forest (Brian Clough) and Ipswich (Alf Ramsey) for the most managers per title. We would need a team winning only one title in their history in a season with two different managers to get lower than 1:1 but Dirk Maas has a more impressive example of a team with one manager per title.

“Since the inception of the Eredivisie in 1956, Feyenoord have secured 11 league titles, won by 11 managers: Jiri Sobotka in 1961, Franz Fuchs in 1962, Wilhelm Kment in 1965, Ben Peeters in 1969, Ernst Happel in 1971, Wiel Coerver in 1974, Thijs Libregts in 1984, Willem van Hanegem in 1993, Leo Beenhakker in 1999, Giovanni van Bronckhorst in 2017 and Arne Slot in 2023.” Alex Ferguson’s haul of 13 league titles over his 26 years in the Manchester United dugout makes United’s titles-per-manager ratio hard to beat and, probably, the definitive answer for fewest managers per title. Rangers have won 55 Scottish league titles with only nine managers for 6.11 titles per manager. That is as close as we could get. If you know of a club with a higher number of titles per manager, get in touch at knowledge@theguardian.com.

In a recent development, “It dawned on me recently that if Chelsea were to go on and win the Europa League this year on 15 May that, for a period of 10 days, they would be the holders of both major European trophies (as well as being technically the holders of the Cup Winners’ Cup),” wrote Brian Quinn in March 2013. “Has there ever been another brief period like this when a team held two European honours simultaneously? Perhaps going back to when there were three distinct European competitions?”.

In a recent development, chelsea will indeed claim a unique honour if they triumph at the Amsterdam Arena in May (spoiler alert: they did). Only four sides have ever won different European competitions in consecutive years – Juventus, Milan, Porto and Liverpool – and in each instance the teams were deposed as holders of one trophy before getting their hands on the other.

Recent findings suggest that milan won the much-missed Cup Winners’ Cup on 23 May 1968, but Slovan Bratislava were crowned the latest champions on 21 May 1969, seven days before Milan hammered Ajax in the Bernabéu to win the 1969 European Cup. Similarly Juventus won the Cup Winners’ Cup on 16 May 1984, but Everton won that tournament almost exactly a year later on 15 May 1985, a fortnight before Juventus won the European Cup in a final overshadowed by the Heysel tragedy.

Likewise, Porto fell a week short in 2002-03 and 2003-04 after winning the Uefa Cup then the Champions League under José Mourinho, as did Liverpool between their Uefa Cup and European Cup wins in 1975-76 and 1976-77.

“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, on Sunday. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”.

“Against the Netherlands this week, Florian Wirtz scored one goal that went in off a post and one that went in off the crossbar. Has anyone ever gone one better and scored a hat-trick with a goal off each post and one off the crossbar?” wonders David Hagan.

It has been revealed that “Seeing Cuba thrash Grenada 9-0 in the Concacaf Nations League, I noted there were eight different scorers (Jorge Aguirre scoring twice). Has any team gone better?” asks Oliver Tuhey.

“My team, Tranmere Rovers, have appeared at Wembley nine times since 1990,” writes David Carruthers. “Can any other team never to have played in the top division beat this?”.

“Are Leicester City the quickest team ever to go from winning the FA Cup to playing in the FA Cup first round proper?” asks Ricardio Sentulio.
